grazalema.intro: Three trees in the Sierra de Grazalema carry a measured sheet in Andalusia's register of singular trees, and each is here for a different reason. A cork oak outside the village once paid, with its cork, for the oil in the lamps of Grazalema's churches. A holm oak at the Puerto de los Acebuches is hollow from age and old charcoal-making. And a lone Spanish fir stands in scrub of strawberry tree and carob near the Pinsapar, the fir forest that is the park's emblem.
grazalema.meta_description: Three singular trees of the Sierra de Grazalema: a cork oak that paid for church lamps, a hollow holm oak 5.40 metres round, a lone pinsapo.
grazalema.question_meta: Nobody has dated a tree in the Sierra de Grazalema. The register's best clue points to a hollow holm oak 5.40 metres round. Three trees, measured.
grazalema.question_answer: No tree in the Sierra de Grazalema has a published age. The strongest clue in Andalusia's register is the hollow holm oak at the Puerto de los Acebuches, 5.40 metres round at chest height, whose sheet calls its hollow trunk an evident sign of great age. It stands beside the A-372 about 6 kilometres from Grazalema, where the Llanos del Rabel trail begins.
grazalema.question_context: Andalusia publishes a measured sheet for each tree in its register of singular trees, and none of the three Grazalema sheets gives an age. What they give instead is size. The holm oak at the Puerto de los Acebuches measures 5.40 metres round at chest height and 7.70 at the base, and the register reads its hollow trunk as the mark of great age and of the charcoal-making that once worked these oaks, concluding that the girth used to be larger still. The Chaparro de las Animas, a cork oak on the edge of Grazalema, is 5.20 metres round with a crown about 24 metres across, and it is the easiest of the three to stand under, since a walk to Campobuche starts at its foot. The pinsapo of El Taramal is slimmer, 2.50 metres round and 20 metres tall, and it is listed for rarity as well as size, because in the Iberian Peninsula the Spanish fir grows wild only in the sierras of Malaga and Cadiz. Reaching it means asking at the El Bosque visitor centre about the permit zone first. If you know the age of any of the three, tell us.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in the Sierra de Grazalema?
faq.a: Nobody has published an age for any of these three. The hollow holm oak at the Puerto de los Acebuches, 5.40 metres round, is the one whose register sheet calls its trunk a sign of great age.

faq.q: Which of these trees can I simply walk to?
faq.a: The Chaparro de las Animas, on public dehesa about 2 kilometres from Grazalema, where a walk to Campobuche starts. The hollow holm oak stands beside the A-372 at a mountain pass. The Taramal pinsapo is in the permit zone of the Pinsapar, so ask at the El Bosque visitor centre before going.

faq.q: Do I need a permit?
faq.a: Around the Pinsapar, yes. Trails there, Llanos del Rabel among them, need a free authorisation from the El Bosque visitor centre and are restricted in the fire season, roughly mid-June to mid-October. The Chaparro de las Animas needs none.

faq.q: What is a pinsapo?
faq.a: Abies pinsapo, the Spanish fir. In the Iberian Peninsula it grows wild only in the sierras of Malaga and Cadiz, and the Pinsapar above Grazalema, the fir forest that is the park's emblem, is one of its strongholds.

cazorla.intro: Four of the five trees here are pines, and in the Sierra de Cazorla they carry stories as much as size. Muleteers once marked the bark of one to tell each other they had passed. Families from the mountain farmhouses heard Sunday Mass under another, and a stone beside a third carries the name of the naturalist who filmed around it. A maritime pine reaches 27 metres near the Fuente del Oso, and two turpentine trees of unusual size grow above the Rio Borosa.
cazorla.meta_description: Five singular trees of the Sierra de Cazorla: the muleteers' pine, the pine of the Mass, the naturalist's pine, a 27-metre maritime pine, turpentine trees.
cazorla.question_meta: No tree in the Sierra de Cazorla has a published age. What Andalusia's register measures instead, and where the five singular trees stand.
cazorla.question_answer: Nobody has published an age for any tree on this page, and Andalusia's register gives none. The thickest trunk it measured at chest height here is the Pino de Felix Rodriguez de la Fuente, a Spanish black pine 4.50 metres round, beside the GR-247 forest track at the Collado de la Zarca, roughly 30 kilometres of track from Cazorla.
cazorla.question_context: The Junta de Andalucia keeps a measured sheet for each tree in its register of singular trees, and for Cazorla those sheets record size, shape and story rather than age. Girth is the nearest thing to a clue, and it has to be read with care, because the sheets measure at different heights. The Felix Rodriguez de la Fuente pine is 4.50 metres round at the standard 1.30 metres. The Pino de la Misa measures about 4.20 metres, but at 40 centimetres above the ground, because it forks so low into three limbs. The Pino de las Cruces, the end point of a waymarked 12.1 kilometre trail from the Puente de las Herrerias, has no girth or height we can give you at all. The maritime pine at the Fuente del Oso is the tallest, at 27 metres, and the turpentine trees above the Rio Borosa are a different species altogether. So this page names no oldest tree. If you know the age of any of them, or have measured the Pino de las Cruces, tell us.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in the Sierra de Cazorla?
faq.a: Nobody has published an age for these five. The thickest trunk measured at chest height is the Pino de Felix Rodriguez de la Fuente, 4.50 metres round.

faq.q: How do I get to the Pino de las Cruces?
faq.a: On foot, along the Junta's waymarked trail from the Puente de las Herrerias, 12.1 kilometres one way, rated high difficulty and about 4 hours 50 minutes each way. Allow a long day.

faq.q: Can I reach these trees by bus?
faq.a: No. All five stand on forest tracks or trails inside the natural park, and none has a bus stop near it. A car, a bike or a long walk is the way in.

faq.q: Why is it called the Pino de la Misa?
faq.a: Because families from the farmhouses of the Sierra once gathered under it on Sundays to celebrate Mass, when the roads to a church were too poor, according to Andalusia's register.

alpujarras.intro: Two trees in Las Alpujarras carry a measured sheet in Andalusia's register of singular trees, and both stand beside mountain roads. A hackberry on the road from Pampaneira to Portugos is 25 metres tall and 8.30 metres round at the base, its trunk looking like two stems fused into one. Higher up, between Busquistar and Trevelez, a Pyrenean oak forks half a metre above the ground and spreads its crown over part of the road.
alpujarras.meta_description: Two singular trees of Las Alpujarras: a hackberry 25 metres tall by the Pampaneira road and a Pyrenean oak whose crown hangs over the road to Trevelez.
alpujarras.question_meta: No tree in Las Alpujarras has a published age. The two singular trees beside its mountain roads, and what Andalusia's register measured.
alpujarras.question_answer: Nobody has published an age for either tree on this page. The bigger of the two is the hackberry at the Fuente del Portillon, 4.75 metres round at chest height and 8.30 at the base, 25 metres tall, beside the road from Pampaneira to Portugos and visible from it.
alpujarras.question_context: Andalusia's register of singular trees gives each of its trees a measured sheet, and neither Alpujarras sheet records an age. Size is all there is to go on, and the two are hard to compare. The hackberry at the Fuente del Portillon was measured at the standard 1.30 metres and is 4.75 metres round there, with ivy over half its trunk. The Pyrenean oak at Las Balsas forks so low that the register measured it at 45 centimetres instead, finding 4.05 metres, so its figure cannot be set beside the hackberry's. They are different species, too, and girth alone says little about age from one species to another. What the two share is the road. Both can be seen from a public road, the hackberry from the one between Pampaneira and Portugos, the oak from the mountain road between Busquistar and Trevelez, where its crown covers part of the carriageway. Neither has a published photograph, so if you drive past, tell us what you see, and if you know how old either is, tell us that too.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Las Alpujarras?
faq.a: Nobody has published an age for either tree here. The larger is the hackberry at the Fuente del Portillon, 8.30 metres round at the base.

faq.q: Can I see them without a hike?
faq.a: Yes. Both stand beside public roads, the hackberry on the Pampaneira to Portugos road and the oak on the road from Busquistar to Trevelez. Stop only where it is safe to pull off.

faq.q: Can I get there without a car?
faq.a: Partly. Pampaneira has a bus from Granada, and the hackberry is a few kilometres from the village along the road to Portugos. The oak at Las Balsas is best reached by car.

aracena.intro: This page holds one tree from the Sierra de Aracena, a Portuguese oak, or quejigo, 27.5 metres tall, growing under the roadside wall below the Pena de Arias Montano above Alajar. Andalusia's register of singular trees lists it for its height. The Pena is the rock where the scholar Benito Arias Montano retired, crowned by a hermitage of medieval origin with a pilgrimage every 8 September, and the area around it holds the natural park's largest stand of quejigo.
aracena.meta_description: A quejigo 27.5 metres tall below the Pena de Arias Montano at Alajar, the Sierra de Aracena's singular tree on this page, and how to reach it.
aracena.question_meta: The Sierra de Aracena tree on this page has no published age. What Andalusia's register says about the tall quejigo of the Pena de Arias Montano.
aracena.question_answer: No age has been published for the one tree on this page, the quejigo below the Pena de Arias Montano. Andalusia's register lists it for its height, 27.5 metres, with a trunk 3.10 metres round at chest height. It stands under the wall of the road up to the Pena, about 1.5 kilometres from Alajar.
aracena.question_context: The quejigo, Quercus faginea, is singled out by the Junta de Andalucia's register for height rather than girth. Its 27.5 metres come from two main limbs that rise almost vertically from the trunk, so the crown, about 17 by 16 metres, is upright rather than spreading. At 3.10 metres round it is no giant by waistline, and the register gives no age. The setting is the other reason to come. The Pena de Arias Montano is a rock outcrop above Alajar where the scholar Benito Arias Montano retired. Its hermitage of Nuestra Senora de los Angeles goes back to medieval times and was remodelled in the sixteenth century, and the pilgrimage to it falls on 8 September. A Junta guide to the area says it holds the largest stand of quejigo in the natural park. This tree grows under the low wall of the road up, among exotic red gum, weeping willow and a few field elms, about 1.5 kilometres from the village by road or by the signed path. If you know its age, tell us.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in the Sierra de Aracena?
faq.a: This page holds one tree from the sierra, and it has no published age. The tall quejigo below the Pena de Arias Montano is listed for its height, 27.5 metres.

faq.q: How do I get to the Pena de Arias Montano?
faq.a: It is about 1.5 kilometres from Alajar, by road or by the signed path from the village. Alajar has a regional bus from Aracena.

faq.q: Does it cost anything?
faq.a: No. The tree stands beside the public road up to the Pena, an open pilgrimage site.

ronda.question_meta: The Castano Santo, possibly 800 years old, is the oldest tree near Ronda. What its measurements actually show, and 9 more in the mountains around it.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree near Ronda?
faq.a: The Castano Santo at Istan, a sweet chestnut that its official register sheet says is possibly around 800 years old. The register uses the word possibly and so does this page.

faq.q: What is a pinsapo?
faq.a: Abies pinsapo, the Spanish fir, a relic fir that survives wild only in three small areas of the mountains behind Ronda and Grazalema. Its needles stand out all round the shoot rather than combing to the sides, which no other European fir does, and its cones stand upright and fall apart on the tree.

faq.q: Are these trees free to visit?
faq.a: Yes, none charges anything. Seven of the ten stand on public land inside the Sierra de las Nieves; for the four on the Quejigales and Saucillo trails, older Junta trail sheets list a park permit that recent guides do not mention, so check the current rules. The other three are on private hillside, two of them a few metres from a public track or bridle path, and one on a crag with no path to its foot, which its entry says plainly.

faq.q: Can you walk between them?
faq.a: Not as one walk. The ten trees are spread across six municipalities, from Cartajima in the Genal valley to Yunquera, reached by mountain road and then on foot. Two pairs make a single outing: the Alcazaba pinsapo and the gall oak of La Plazoleta stand about a kilometre apart above the Puerto de los Pilones, and the Pinsapo Moreno and the Candelabra Pinsapo lie on the same trail from the Puerto del Saucillo above Yunquera. Treat the rest as separate days out from Ronda.

faq.q: How reliable are the measurements?
faq.a: They are the best on this site. Andalusia publishes a one-page sheet for each singular tree giving total height, clear trunk height, girth at 1.30 metres, girth at the base, crown diameter in two directions and crown area, plus a note on ownership and surroundings. Every figure on this page comes from those sheets.

granada.intro: Granada plants its trees the way it builds its gardens: behind walls, inside monastery grounds, up palace hillsides, rarely as an afterthought. A mystic poet planted one with his own hands while awaiting canonisation of a very different kind. A tree measured decades before botanists had formally described its own species grows two centuries downhill of that. The city has never compiled a tree register of its own, so this list draws on scattered research, plus two trees outside town from Andalusia's regional register.
granada.meta_description: Granada's 11 most remarkable trees, from a 440-year-old cypress planted by a mystic poet to Generalife sequoias older than their own species' discovery.
granada.question_meta: Granada's oldest tree: a 440-year-old cypress at Carmen de los Martires, planted by poet San Juan de la Cruz. Its story and ten more remarkable trees.
granada.question_context: Granada has no municipal tree register of its own, so this list draws on scattered research: a magazine-published survey of twelve singular trees across the city, the Alhambra and Generalife's own heritage documentation, the University of Granada Botanical Garden's records of its own founding-era specimens, and, for two trees just outside the city, Andalusia's regional register of singular trees. Within that combined pool, the cypress of San Juan de la Cruz at Carmen de los Martires is the one most precisely dated, on the strength of a documented six-year residency (1582-1588) by the Carmelite mystic, rather than a vaguer estimate. Some popular sources round the tree's age up to 500 years; this site uses the more conservative, better-documented figure tied to San Juan de la Cruz's own recorded time at the convent, itself older than the Generalife's own sequoias or the botanical garden's ginkgo, both 19th century plantings by comparison. The garden is free and open to the public, a short walk from the Alhambra.

cordoba.intro: Cordoba keeps its oldest trees behind walls, or out of town. The city's public gardens were laid out in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, so its own catalogue of singular trees is full of magnificent specimens only eighty or ninety years old. The genuinely ancient ones stand in a cathedral courtyard, a palace garden and, nine kilometres north, beside the Canada Real Soriana drove road, where a carob is put at 350 to 400 years. What the city has in abundance is scale and scent, from a plane reaching thirty-seven metres to a courtyard of bitter oranges.
cordoba.question_answer: The oldest documented tree in Cordoba is the olive beside the fountain in the Patio de los Naranjos, the orange courtyard of the Mezquita-Catedral. It already appears on a plan of the courtyard drawn in 1741, which makes it around 285 years old, a date that rests on a document rather than an estimate. The Patio is free to enter daily, so this is one ancient tree that costs nothing to stand in front of.
cordoba.question_context: Half of its trunk is gone. The tree hollowed through the twentieth century and decayed badly from the 1980s, so what leans toward the fountain today is a shell that still produces about sixty kilos of olives a year. In 2018 researchers sampled its leaves and fruit without harming it and found a local cultivar barely recorded anywhere else, which they have proposed naming after the city. Tourist copy sometimes calls the tree a thousand years old; there is no basis for that, and the 1741 plan is the actual evidence. Two trees may be older, on weaker evidence. The holm oak in the garden of the Palacio de Viana, which rises above the roofline at over twenty-five metres, has stood for four centuries by the palace's own word rather than any survey. Nine kilometres north of the centre, a carob beside the Canada Real Soriana drove road is put at 350 to 400 years by Andalusia's register of singular trees, which does not say how it reached that figure. Everything else in the city is younger than it looks.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Cordoba?
faq.a: The oldest documented one is the olive beside the fountain in the Patio de los Naranjos, around 285 years old and drawn on a 1741 plan of the courtyard. It survives on half a trunk and still fruits. Free to visit, daily.

faq.q: When does the orange blossom in Cordoba?
faq.a: The azahar peaks in late March and early April, and the scent lasts roughly a month on the tree. The exact date shifts every year with the weather, so nobody can promise you a week.

faq.q: Does Cordoba have really ancient trees?
faq.a: Three, honestly. The Mezquita olive is documented on a 1741 plan; the Viana holm oak is four centuries old by the palace's account; and a carob north of the city is put at 350 to 400 years by Andalusia's register. The rest of the city's remarkable trees are mostly eighty to a hundred and thirty years old, because its public gardens were laid out in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

faq.q: Which of these are free to see?
faq.a: All but two. The Patio de los Naranjos with its olive, the Orive garden, the Agriculture Gardens, the Alpargate plane and the cemetery Judas tree cost nothing. The Viana holm oak is inside a paid museum.

malaga.intro: Malaga's most remarkable trees rarely come from the wild. Almost every one on this list arrived as an import, an accident, or a rescue: a fig mistaken for a magnolia, an olive dug up whole from a neighbouring town, an avocado planted a century and a half ago. The city joined a European tagging scheme in 2022 to mark ten of them with plaques, and this list draws on that selection, the botanical garden collecting since 1855, and an ombu in the Montes de Malaga.
malaga.meta_description: Malaga's ten most remarkable trees, from a 400-year-old transplanted olive to a fig beside a Picasso sculpture. Locations, stories, how to reach each one.
malaga.question_meta: Malaga's oldest tree: a 400-year-old olive at La Concepcion garden, moved whole from Velez-Malaga. Its story, location, and nine more remarkable trees.
malaga.question_context: Malaga does not have a single dominant tree register the way some cities do. Its strongest source is a 2022 municipal scheme, run under the European TreeTags project and the international Tree Cities of the World programme, which tagged ten specimens across the city as singular for their size, age or location. Separately, the Jardin Botanico-Historico La Concepcion, a private estate opened to the public and declared a historic garden in 1943, keeps its own record of a dozen outsized trees inherited from more than a century of collecting, and Andalusia's regional register adds an ombu in the Montes de Malaga. Within that combined pool, the Concepcion's olive tree is the one most consistently described as the city's oldest, on the strength of a roughly 400-year age estimate given by the garden itself, though as with most veteran olives, the figure is a general estimate rather than a ring count. The garden sits at the northern edge of the city, a paid site (small entry fee), reachable by bus from the centre.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Malaga?
faq.a: The olive tree of the Jardin Botanico-Historico La Concepcion, estimated at around 400 years old and moved there whole from Velez-Malaga. It grows in the garden's Mediterranean plant collection, a paid site north of the city centre.

faq.q: What is Malaga's TreeTags scheme?
faq.a: A 2022 municipal programme, part of the European TreeTags project and the international Tree Cities of the World initiative, that placed identifying plaques on ten trees across Malaga chosen for their size, age or location. Five of the trees on this list carry one of those tags.

faq.q: Are Malaga's remarkable trees free to see?
faq.a: Yes, apart from one ticket. Everything here stands in free public parks, gardens and streets, or on the public forest tracks of the Montes de Malaga, except the trees inside the Jardin Botanico-Historico La Concepcion, which charge a small entry fee.

faq.q: Why are so many of Malaga's oldest trees not native to Spain?
faq.a: Most arrived through 19th and 20th century fashion and trade: wealthy estate owners and municipal gardeners planting species from Australia, South America and Asia because they had just become available, not because they grow wild in Andalusia. The city's one native oak on this list stands out for being the exception.
